scenes.text: Here's a common pattern. A council worries that local teenagers hardly exercise. It spends two hundred thousand dollars on an outdoor gym in the main park, good equipment, free to use, opened with a photo in the local paper. Eighteen months later, it's almost unused. Nothing is broken. Write down four reasons it might be empty. Then, what should the council have done before it spent the money?

The Ottawa Charter, from nineteen eighty-six, is the framework Australian health promotion is built around. Its five action areas aren't five kinds of campaign. They're five levels where you can act, each answering a question. Build healthy public policy: what are the rules and prices? Create supportive environments: what are the settings people live, learn and play in? Strengthen community action: who decides? Develop personal skills: what do people know and can do? And reorient health services: what is the health system for?

Reorienting health services is the one students get wrong. It doesn't mean building more hospitals. It means changing what the system is for and how it works: funding prevention, moving services into the community, and redesigning them so the people with most need can actually use them. A youth health service with no appointment, no referral, no cost, and a waiting room that doesn't feel like a hospital, is reorienting a service. A bigger emergency department isn't.

Alongside the action areas, the Charter names three strategies. The action areas are where you act. The strategies are how. Enable means giving people the resources and opportunity to reach their potential, like free transport where there's no bus. Mediate means reconciling competing interests, like a council's revenue, residents' sleep and alcohol harm. Advocate means making health a public priority. Mediation explains why health promotion is slow. Almost every structural change has someone who loses by it.

Now the gym. The council used one action area, a supportive environment, and it wasn't the one holding things back. No community action: nobody asked teenagers what they wanted, or where they'd use it. No personal skills: a row of equipment isn't self-explanatory, and nobody wants to look foolish in a public park. No policy change about lighting or whether teenagers are welcome. No service or club linked to keep it alive. And was the environment really supportive? Is it reachable without a car, lit, and safe for young women in the evening? The first fix was to ask, which is community action, and it's free.

Compare that with how the Charter has actually improved Australia's health. Tobacco control filled several rows at once: tax and plain packaging as policy, smoke-free venues as environments, quitting support built into health services, and education building skills. For young people, the same rows hold graduated licensing, school canteen rules, and free or low-cost youth mental health centres. So, to judge any initiative, run it through all five rows, and name the empty ones.

Community action is the row most often claimed and least often done. Remember the participation ladder: informed, consulted, partner, and lead, where the community has control. Consultation asks. Control decides. Real partnership, shared decisions and resources, changes outcomes for three reasons. Relevance: a community knows its own barriers, so it solves the real problem, not the visible one. Trust and reach: young people who avoid institutions still talk to someone they know. And durability: a program a community owns keeps going when the funding round ends.

The syllabus asks about partnerships across a range of cultural groups. For Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples, the clearest form is the community-controlled health sector, and national agreements made with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander representatives, built on the premise that programs designed without communities hadn't worked. The same principle applies elsewhere. Migrant and refugee communities often work with bilingual community health workers, so information and services actually fit. In each case, the community holds real decisions.

Last time's three approaches fit inside the Charter. Policy, environments and community action act on conditions, which is the socio-ecological approach. Personal skills keep the behavioural approach as one part, not the whole. And reorienting services asks the biomedical system to look upstream. Students lose marks three ways: listing the five without applying them, forcing all five when an initiative used three, and calling advocacy an action area, when it's a strategy.
Two things to remember. To judge any initiative, name the empty rows. And consultation asks, control decides.

Two exam questions. First. A hypothetical state makes bicycle helmets compulsory for riders under eighteen. Identify the Ottawa Charter action area this uses, and outline actions in two other action areas that would increase its effect. Pause here to answer.

It's healthy public policy, changing the rules for everyone. To add to it, create supportive environments, like safe, separated cycleways near schools, and develop personal skills, like bike safety lessons and fitting checks. Or strengthen community action, with a youth group helping plan the routes. The classic mistake is naming advocacy, which is a strategy, not an action area.
Second. Explain how the action areas of the Ottawa Charter are used to promote the health of young people in Australia. Pause here to answer.

Name the Charter as the nineteen eighty-six WHO framework. Then give each action area a young-people example and what it changes: graduated licensing, canteen rules, youth advisory groups, health lessons at school, and youth health centres. Then say why they're used together: each covers what the others can't reach. The classic mistake is a generic list that could be about anyone.

So, run any initiative through five rows, name the empty ones, and check who held the decisions. Next, we zoom out from one charter to seventeen global goals. If only one is about health, why do the other sixteen matter?
